Empirical Research Plan  
“Access to Medicaid and Adult Mortality, 1990-2015”

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
Primary method: Difference-in-Differences (DiD) with staggered adoption, estimated as (i) a two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) event-study and (ii) the Callaway-Sant’Anna (2021) group-time ATT estimator to avoid the TWFE heterogeneity bias.  

Why appropriate?  
• Treatment (state Medicaid expansion eligibility for low-income adults) switched on at different dates across states, creating plausibly exogenous policy shocks.  
• Individual-level linked NHIS–NDI panel delivers pre- and post-outcome measures for treated and never/late treated units.  
• Annual frequency (1990–2015) allows rich pre-trend tests and dynamic mortality effects.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
Tist = 1 if individual i in state s is observed in year t after the state’s Medicaid expansion took effect *and* the individual’s family income ≤ 138% FPL (mirrors ACA rule and ensures low-income focus). Otherwise 0.

Control group / counterfactual  
A. Never-treated or not-yet-treated low-income individuals in states that had not expanded by year t.  
B. Robustness: individuals in the same state with slightly higher income (138–200% FPL) who are ineligible—“in-state higher-income control”.

Treatment timing  
Expansion (event) date = first calendar year the state made low-income adults without categorical restrictions eligible for Medicaid (e.g., Section 1115 early waivers, ACA 2014 expansions, etc.). We record exact month but aggregate to post-year ≥ exp.year.

No RDD is involved; the running variable is time to expansion in the event-study specification.

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Parallel trends: absent the policy, mortality trends of low-income adults would have been similar across expansion and non-expansion states.  
Plausibility: Pre-ACA, no systematic mortality divergence is documented; we will test visually and with placebo leads.

A2. No differential anticipatory behavior: individuals can’t change current mortality risk simply because their state announced reform one year ahead. Short announcement-to-implementation lags support this.

A3. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): mortality of an individual is unaffected by another state’s expansion. Cross-state migration of low-income adults is low (Census), lending support.

A4. Composition stability: the set of low-income adults in NHIS within a state-year does not change systematically because of the expansion itself (or we can control for observables and weight survey). Plausible; we will test for shifts in age, sex, and race shares.

A5. Accurate treatment coding: Expansion dates and eligibility thresholds are correctly coded (we will use Kaiser Family Foundation timeline and CMS waiver documents).

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats & Mitigation  

T1. Violation of parallel trends due to coincident state health policies (e.g., tobacco taxes, insurance exchanges).  
Mitigation: State×year controls for concurrent policies; include state-specific linear trends; robustness to removing states with large contemporaneous reforms.

T2. Selective migration of sick individuals into expansion states.  
Mitigation: Use NHIS self-reported state‐of‐birth to flag movers; re-estimate on non-movers; show migration flows of low-income adults are negligible (<1%/yr).

T3. Treatment misclassification / take-up imperfect.  
Mitigation: Instrument individual Medicaid enrollment with state-level eligibility (2SLS) as robustness; show first-stage F-stat > 20.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # DiD / TWFE / event study
library(did)          # Callaway–Sant’Anna
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data --------------------------------------------------------------
nhis <- fread("NHIS_NDI_1990_2015.csv")        # individual-level
exp  <- fread("state_medicaid_expansion_dates.csv")  # expansion timing

# 2. Merge & construct variables -------------------------------------------
setkey(nhis, state, year)
setkey(exp , state)
nhis <- exp[nhis]                              # adds expansion_year

nhis[, post  := as.integer(year >= expansion_year)]
nhis[, treat := as.integer(post == 1 & income_fpl <= 138)]
nhis[, ever_treated := as.integer(!is.na(expansion_year))]

# Event-time dummies (–5 to +6, omitting –1)
for (k in -5:6) nhis[, paste0("e",k) := as.integer(year - expansion_year == k)]

# Outcome: all-cause mortality within 1 year of survey
nhis[, death := as.integer(death_within_12m == 1)]

# Survey weights
w <- "survey_weight"

# 3. TWFE DiD ---------------------------------------------------------------
twfe <- feols(death ~ treat | state + year, data = nhis,
              weights = nhis[[w]], cluster = ~state)
summary(twfe)

# 4. Event-study ------------------------------------------------------------
event_vars <- paste0("e", -5:6)[-6]  # drop e-1
formula_ev <- as.formula(
  paste("death ~", paste(event_vars, collapse = " + "), "| state + year")
)
est_ev <- feols(formula_ev, data = nhis, weights = nhis[[w]], cluster = ~state)

iplot(est_ev, ref.line = -1, xlab = "Years since expansion", ylab = "ATT on mortality")

# 5. Callaway–Sant’Anna estimator ------------------------------------------
cs <- att_gt(yname = "death", tname = "year", idname = "id",
             gname = "expansion_year", xformla = ~ age + sex + race,
             data = nhis[ever_treated==1 | year < 2014],  # truncate if desired
             est_method = "dr", panel = FALSE)            # NHIS repeated cross-section
agg_effects <- aggte(cs, type = "dynamic")
summary(agg_effects)
ggdid(agg_effects)

# 6. Robustness: placebos (advance treatment date by 5y) -------------------
nhis[, placebo_post := as.integer(year >= expansion_year - 5)]
nhis[, placebo_treat := as.integer(placebo_post == 1 & income_fpl <= 138)]
placebo <- feols(death ~ placebo_treat | state + year, data = nhis,
                 weights = nhis[[w]], cluster = ~state)
summary(placebo)   # expect ~0

```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results (Prior)  
Economic theory (access to preventive and acute care) predicts Medicaid lowers mortality. Existing estimates (Oregon Lottery, ACA Medicaid) suggest a 0.1–0.2 ppt (5–10 %) reduction in annual mortality among 45–64 low-income adults. We therefore expect:

ATT ≈ –0.15 percentage points in 1-year mortality (baseline mean ≈ 1.5 %), i.e., a 10 % decline, growing over time (–0.3 ppt after 5 years).

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist (Self-Assessment, DiD)

C1. Parallel pre-trends documented (pre-coefficients ≈ 0): 1  
C2. No anticipation (placebo leads insignificant): 1  
C3. No time-varying confounders (controls & trends): 0.5  
C4. Stable sample composition / no selective migration: 0.5  
C5. Correctly implemented staggered DiD estimator (CS/Goodman-Bacon diagnostics): 1  

Total = 4 / 5 → Reasonably credible, with residual concern about concurrent policies and migration.

------------------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
